subject: Re: [stan-users] Latent variables in hierarchical model

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Latent variables in hierarchical model
parts:
Sorry nobody answered this back in July when you sent it out.
I'll try to answer some things inline.

Hopefully better late than never.


> On Jul 19, 2016, at 6:02 AM, liam....@gmail.com wrote:
>
> Hi all,
>
>
> I'm pretty new to Stan (and HMC/NUTS in general). My question is geared towards Stan, but it may be that the issue is more general than that.
>
>
>
> I'm trying to fit a model with a somewhat elaborate hierarchical form:
>
>
>
> y ~ bernoulli_logit( alpha+V*beta+Z*gamma )
>
>
>
> where Z is a kind of "latent" variable with Z ~ normal( W*tau, sigma1 )
>
>
>
> As with any typical regression, I have an N-dimensional response vector (y) and a matrix of predictor variables (X).
>
> I split the matrix of predictor variables (X) into two distinct and non-overlapping sub-matrices (V and W).
>
> V denotes a matrix with P columns and N rows.
>
> W denotes a matrix with Q columns and N rows. Along with a scale parameter sigma1, the Q columns of W are used to parametrise a "latent" variable (Z) which, when realised, is combined with the above V matrix to form a linear predictor for the response vector y.
>
>
>
> Hopefully, the following R code will be illustrative.
>
>
>
> ##########
>
>
>
> # SIMULATE FROM MODEL:
>
>
>
> # Predictors:
>
> X <- matrix( rnorm(6000), nrow=1000 ) # Predictor matrix.
>
> V <- X[,1:3] # Observed predictors.
>
> W <- X[,4:6] # Predictors of latent variable.
>
>
>
> # Initialise parameters:
>
> alpha <- 3 # Observed intercept.
>
> beta <- c(3,7,-6) # Observed slopes.
>
> tau <- c(2,3,-5) # Latent slopes.
>
> gamma <- 2 # Slope for latent variate.
>
> sigma1 <- 1.1 # Scale parameter for latent variable.
>
>
>
> # Simulate from Z:
>
> expected_Z <- W%*%tau # Mean for latent variable Z.
>
> Z <- rnorm(1000, expected_Z, sigma1) # Simulate Z from normal distribution with mean expected_Z and scale sigma1.
>
>
>
> # Simulate from y:
>
> lin_pred <- alpha + V%*%beta + gamma*Z # Linear predictor for y.
>
> pr <- 1/(1 + exp(-lin_pred)) # Map from (-inf, inf) to [0,1]; inverse logit.
>
> y <- rbinom(1000, 1, pr) # Simulate y from Bernoulli distribution with “success” parameter pr.
>
>
>
> ##########
>
>
>
> My attempt to fit this model using Stan doesn't appear to be very effective. Aside from posterior distributions which don't seem to characterise the initialized values above, n_eff is very low and Rhat is well above 1.
>
>
>
> The Stan code is:
>
>
>
> /* BEGIN STAN CODE: */
>
>
>
> data {
>
>
>
> int<lower=0> N; // # observations.
>
> int<lower=0> P; // # predictors in V matrix.
>
> int<lower=0> Q; // # predictors in W matrix.
>
>
>
> int<lower=0,upper=1> y[N]; // Response.
>
> matrix[N,P] V; // Observed predictors.
>
> matrix[N,Q] W; // Latent predictors.
>
>
>
> }
>
>
>
> parameters {
>
>
>
> vector[Q] tau; // Latent slope(s).
>
> real alpha; // Observed intercept.
>
> vector[P] beta; // Observed slope(s).
>
> real<lower=0> gamma; // Slope for latent variate.
>
>
>
> real sigma1; // Scale parameter for latent variable.
>
>
>
> vector[N] Z; // Latent variable.
>
>
>
> }
>
>
>
> model {
>
>
>
> vector[N] expected_Z; // Declare mean for latent variable Z.
>
> vector[N] lin_pred; // Declare linear predictor.
>
> expected_Z <- W*tau; // Initialize mean for latent variable Z (combination of latent predictors).
>
> Z ~ normal(expected_Z,sigma1); // Draw Z from distribution.
>
> lin_pred <- alpha + V*beta + Z*gamma; // Initialize linear predictor for y.
>
> y ~ bernoulli_logit(lin_pred); // Compute log probability.
>

You can just use these directly --- you don't need to
define local variables. e.g.,

Z ~ normal(W * tau, sigma1);

>
>
> }
>
>
>
> /* END STAN CODE: */
>
>
>
> A few things:
>
>
>
> - For the moment, I'm relying on the implicit built-in uniform priors in Stan for all model parameters; of course, placing informative priors on the parameters will alter the posterior distributions, but I want to see how the model performs in the absence of informative priors. The adapted continuous model (see below) performs very well with just the uniform priors on all parameters.

A flat prior is more informative than you may hope. It's saying
almost all the values to be expected are extreme because there's
only finite mass inside any compact volume.

> - I've constrained the parameter gamma to non-negative values and I have neglected to include an intercept value in the expected_Z term in the interest of ensuring an identifiable model. Perhaps I haven't gone far enough in this direction? Is the model under-constrained?

Maybe. You can look at pairs plots to see if there
are additively correlated (lines) or multiplicatively
correlated (bananas) paramters.

> - When I alter the structure of the predictor variables to contain dummy/binary variables (i.e. values in {0, 1}) and/or constrained values (e.g. values in [-1,1]), maximum tree depth issues begin to arise; is this a common issue for these kinds of variables?

No, but if you have uniform priors and run into things like
separability issues, it can be a problem.

> - When I change the structure of the model to have a continuous response (i.e. y ~ normal( alpha+V*beta+Z*gamma, sigma2 ), where sigma2 is a scale parameter for the response variable), the results become much better, so I'm guessing that the issue may lie with bernoulli_logit response.

Yes, that changes the response dramatically. You no longer
get a separability problem where some parameters will try to
grow infinitely large.

>
> - Noting the above, according to this post, a transformation based on the normal distribution might be appropriate, but I'm not sure that these cases are like-for-like. Could anybody elaborate on this?

Not sure what kind of transformation you're talking about here.

> - In general, does anybody have any suggestions as to how I could improve the code to recover posterior distributions more representative of the values above?

I'd simulate data to see if the model's correct. It may just
be misspecified for the model.

Also, we highly recommend at least weakly informative priors.

> This post seems to have expanded beyond the compact form that I had originally intended for it. Sorry about that.

Longer posts tend not to get answered because it's too hard
to figure out the models and all the questions. Sorry this one
took me so long.

- Bob
